Impact of Algorithm Choice

September 1, 2020

AlgorithmsPerformance

This page tests three variants of matrix–matrix multiplication and reports their execution times below.

All three algorithms implement the same specification. Consider two matrices, A and B, with dimensions M × K and K × N, respectively. Their product, C, is computed by multiplying and adding the elements in each row of A with the elements in each column of B, producing M × N values.

This gives us the familiar loop structure:

for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
  for (j = 0; j < N; j++)
    for (k = 0; k < K; k++)
      C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]

Changing the order of these loops does not change the final result. The three variants below come from reordering the loops while leaving the update statement unchanged.

  1. Fully update — textbook algorithm
    Loop order: i, j, k
    Each element of C is fully computed before the algorithm moves to another element. Assuming row-major storage for A and B, accesses to A are sequential while accesses to B are strided.
  2. Fully update — loops switched
    Loop order: j, i, k
    Each element of C is again fully computed before the algorithm moves on. Assuming row-major storage, accesses to B are sequential while accesses to A are strided.
  3. Partial update
    Loop order: k, i, j
    Each element of C is only partially computed before the algorithm moves to the next element. Assuming row-major storage, accesses to A and B are sequential in the innermost loop.

Test the variants

Are the results what you expect? Think about why the execution times may differ even though the variants are mathematically equivalent.

Timings vary by browser and machine. Run the test a few times to get a sense of the average behavior.
